summary: Help 4–6-year-olds recognise and name common 2-D shapes (circle, triangle, rectangle, square) by their DEFINING FEATURES — a triangle is a closed figure with three straight sides — rather than by matching a single remembered 'prototype' picture. Young children build each category around a prototype (an equilateral, horizontal-based triangle; a long, brick-like rectangle) and wrongly reject valid non-prototypical cases (long-thin, right, obtuse or point-down triangles) and mis-name a tilted square as a 'diamond'. Teach with many VARIED examples (sizes, orientations, proportions, colours) shown together, carefully chosen NON-examples, precise naming, and asking the child to say WHY each figure is or isn't the shape.
misconceptions: Judges a shape only against a visual prototype: accepts the equilateral, horizontal-based triangle but rejects long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down triangles (non-prototypical TYPES are hardest — about half of children miss isosceles and right triangles).
Treats ORIENTATION as if it defines the shape: a square rotated 45° is called a 'diamond' not a square; a triangle without a horizontal base is rejected.
Names by overall resemblance to an object (a 'roof', a 'mountain') rather than by counting straight sides and corners.
Uses 'diamond' for a rotated square, rhombus or kite — there is no 2-D shape called a diamond.

activities.title: Catch every triangle (varied-case shape hunt)
steps: Look at a field of many shapes that mixes tidy triangles with long-thin, tilted and point-down triangles, plus near-miss non-examples such as a figure with one curved side and three lines that do not quite close.
Tap/pick out every triangle you can find, including the ones that look unusual.
After choosing, say for one of the unusual ones WHY it is a triangle (e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up').
Say why a near-miss is NOT a triangle (its side is curved, or it isn't closed).
activities.insight: Sameness of a shape lives in its features — three straight sides and a closed figure — not in its size, proportions, or which way it points. A long, thin, upside-down triangle belongs to the same family as the tidy one.

activities.title: Is it or not? — and how do you know?
steps: For each figure the teacher shows or draws, decide: is this a triangle (or circle, rectangle, square) — yes or no?

Say out loud which feature makes you sure: count the straight sides, check it is closed, and point to each corner (for rectangles and squares, also check the corners are square corners, and for a square that all four sides are the same length).
Work through deliberately tricky cases: an unclosed figure, a figure with a curved side, a tilted square, and a triangle with no horizontal base.

Sort a mixed set of cut-out shapes into groups and justify the borderline cases. (The cut-outs are thin cards that stand in for the flat shapes we mean — look at the outline, its sides and corners, not the card's thickness.)
activities.insight: Deciding and explaining — not just naming the obvious prototype — is what reveals and repairs prototype and orientation thinking. The reason ('three straight sides, closed') matters as much as the answer.

activities.title: Turn the same shape (orientation does not change identity)
steps: Hold one cut-out square and slowly rotate it: at each turn answer 'Is it still a square now? And now?' (The card is a thin stand-in for the flat square — watch its outline, not its thickness.)
Check that the number of straight sides and corners does not change as the shape turns.
Rotate a triangle until its point is at the bottom and confirm it is still a triangle.
Notice that a square turned 45° is still a square. 'Diamond' is an everyday word, not the mathematical name for this shape, so we call it a square.
activities.insight: Turning a shape does not change what it is; identity is invariant over orientation because the sides and corners stay the same. 'Diamond' is an everyday word, not the mathematical shape name — a rotated square is still a square.

activities.title: Sort-and-justify check (tricky cases)
steps: Drag or place figures into 'triangle' and 'not a triangle' groups, where the 'triangle' group must include long-thin and point-down positives and the 'not' group includes a curved-sided near-miss.
Answer 'Which of these are still squares?' when one option is a tilted (correct) square.
For each tricky choice, give the feature-based reason.
Transfer: find another triangle that looks very different from the first but is still a triangle.
activities.insight: A child who reasons from features will accept non-prototypical positives AND reject near-miss non-examples for the right reason; the 'how do you know' part distinguishes feature reasoning from prototype or object reasoning.

checkQuestion: Put out a mixed set of cut-out shapes including a tidy triangle, a long thin triangle, a triangle turned so its point is at the bottom, a tilted square, a circle, and a near-miss with one curved side. Say: 'Show me all the triangles.' Then point to the point-down triangle and to the curved-sided near-miss in turn and ask: 'How do you know this one is / isn't a triangle?'
checkAnswer: Picks every triangle regardless of size, proportion or orientation (including the long-thin and point-down ones), leaves out the circle, the tilted square and the curved-sided near-miss, and justifies by the defining feature — 'it has three straight sides and it's closed' — not by how it looks or which way it points.
